title: Lee Simpson (founder of Jefferson City Buzzards) Interview, 1948-06-09
interviewee: Lee Simpson (founder of Jefferson City Buzzards)

blocks.x: We are gathered here at the clubhouse of the Jefferson City Partners Carnival Club. Mr. Simpson, as much as you are the last surviving member of the original group who founded the Jefferson City Partners, we younger members of the club have come to you for some really authentic first-hand information, and we feel certain that you will give it to us for the best of your ability. We are prompted to do this because we believe that the fighters will continue as the granddaddy of the marching clubs around New Orleans for many, many years to come. So what you tell us here this evening, incidentally, which is Wednesday, June 9, 1948, will be of untold historical value to the club or into the future. As signatories to this interview, I think we should all identify ourselves. I am Mark Wiley, and this is...
Thank you. Marley's case, Elliman. And here is Mr. Simpson. You want Mr. Toto? I asked him to correct you so I can answer.
This is Lee Simpson, one of the original members of the club, the only man of the old time and that it arrives today.
And the, uh... It's Brother Mark, another old member. Thank you, Mark. Um, Mr. Simpson, will you give us a short background sketch of yourself? Thank you.

Brother Simpson, did you tell the boys about the terrain we had on the trees these nights? That we went to Brother Lock's house and had some boiled wine, and what happened to our field family when we was coming up Camp Street? How is? We visited our grand morse's house, Mr. Louis Lock. And they had enough of stuff there to float a steamboat. And some of the boys imagined that they were steamboats. And got tanked up. And we had at that time the Burgeon's drum and five-coats from both the members of the Burgeon. And in particular, a man by the name of Adam Habs, who was a member of the club, he was the bass drum player. And he picked the bass drum so much that he got dizzy and fell down. And he had to pick him up and put him in a wagon and bring him home.
That is one of the incidents of the Lock's visit.

And when we struck Petit Avenue and Law Street, going up to Marfell's to make our formation, Brother Wilmer, my Brother Wilmer, jumped, there was a bunch of niggers, little niggers on the corner, and he jumped out and made like he got to grab one, and the nigger got to fits. And it was a time waking on to bring him to. Uh, Brother Simpson, maybe you can give us a few details on the time we paraded with a fire truck when you run into Brother Ziggler's garden with it. Yes, the year we paraded with the fire engine on our way to disappearing that evening, we visited Brother members of the club by the name of Ziggler, who lived on Petit Avenue and Law. He was a gardener, had a large hothouse, and it seemed like some of the boys that were pulling the engine, they took the two niggers out of the engine and pulled it in his yard by hand. I don't know what the idea was, or going in there, but anyway, instead of taking the road, they went through his hothouse. Brother Simpson, can you give us an idea what the ground for this club cost? At the cost of the ground, we perched it from a Negro brick mason by the name of Monroe Wilson, who lived right around the corner from the club on Bellcastle between Law and Lunciation, and gave him $225 for the ground. Add a small building in the back, two rooms and little shed to it, and we demolished that. Brother Simpson, isn't it true that we tried to get the lot up at the next corner of, uh, what's it? On Falmore's enunciation, and they had some hitch in the owner, the title? Prior to getting this piece of ground where the clubhouse is situated now, we tried to get a piece of ground up there on, uh, on, uh, enunciation in Vermont Street. But after an investigation, we found out there was some defect in the title, so we left the loan and bought this place. Uh, Brother Thurston, can you let us know some of the games that we had at the ground? Yes. I know. I know. I know. I know. I know. I know. I know. I know. I know. I know. the dead eppy club. We used to have regular games at the club here every Saturday night and Sunday. Poker games. And the man that used to take charge of the poker games and run them for us was a member of ours by the name of Joe Schweitzer.
And he blocked them out at the New Orleans Ball Ball.

And his request on several occasions while them the clubhouse playing cards, he says the ball the He says, boys, if I die, don't fail to put a deck of cards in my coffin. And we did fail. A deck of cards went in his coffin. I guess he's playing cards with him today. I'll now transfer you over to Brother Worldly.
Well, Mr. Simpson, it's been a great deal of pleasure to all of us to have you here tonight, and I'm sure this record that's been made will be appreciated by many future members. Good night.

Well, brothers, I'm happy to be with you tonight, and it's more than a pleasure to you to give any information, whatever I can remember, concerning the club. And if I've made any mistake, it's not my fault. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
